..
Issued at 252 PM CDT Thu Jul 23 2026

The September-like air mass that has settled into the region 
will stick around for yet another day tomorrow. A third 
consecutive day of air mass warming paired with modest return 
flow on the backside of a departing ~1022 mb surface high will
likely allow for at least a few low 80s air temperature 
readings to be observed tomorrow afternoon amidst a mix of 
sunshine and clouds, with upper 70s high temperatures expected
otherwise. Dew points will also increase from what they were 
today, but humidity levels should nevertheless still remain in 
a comfortable range tomorrow.

A couple of shortwave troughs will track east-southeastward 
tonight into tomorrow from the Great Plains towards the 
Mississippi and Ohio river valleys and will be accompanied by 
rain in some areas. The northernmost of these waves will pass 
over or track very near our CWA and will likely induce enough 
saturation in the middle and upper levels of the troposphere to 
support precipitation in the associated cloud layer over or very
near our southern counties. However, descending hydrometeors 
will have to work through a robust dry sub-cloud layer 
(initially over 10000 ft deep), and this may prove to be
difficult to overcome in the absence of stronger forcing aloft.
Thus, while some sprinkles could be observed in some of our 
southernmost locales during the daytime tomorrow, measurable 
precipitation appears unlikely to occur.

After this shortwave disturbance departs, a plume of meager 
instability will lift northeastward into the region Friday night
into Saturday morning. While lapse rates will remain 
unimpressive during this time frame, increasing low-level 
moisture may nevertheless allow for some shower activity to 
sprout within the associated wing of warm air advection/isentropic
ascent -- primarily across our southern counties and points 
farther to the south. Opted to introduce slight chance PoPs to
the gridded forecast database across the southern half or so of
our forecast area for the overnight Friday into Saturday 
morning time frame to account for this possibility. If any cells
associated with this activity manage to grow tall enough, then 
a few isolated lightning strikes could also occur. Otherwise, 
conditions should dry out for Saturday afternoon as the 
associated forcing progresses eastward and strengthening capping
quashes any attempts from surface-based air parcels to freely 
convect within an increasingly moist/humid air mass.

By Sunday, a much more July-like air mass will become established
across the region with air temperatures building into the upper
80s and 90s and evapotranspirationally-supplemented dew points 
climbing solidly into the 70s (and possibly even near 80F in 
spots) as an upper-level ridge strengthens and expands across 
the central third of the CONUS. Heat indices in our area are 
thus likely to eclipse the century mark and could potentially 
rise high enough to warrant heat headlines for at least part of 
our forecast area on Sunday and possibly again on Monday as well.

This muggy air mass will also be primed for thunderstorm 
activity. Particularly, the consistent model signal for multiple
shortwaves navigating around the top of the aforementioned 
ridge and diving into the moist and strongly unstable air mass 
present across the Upper Midwest/Great Lakes amidst strong 
northwesterly flow does raise concern for one or more severe to 
potentially destructive convective complexes tracking through 
the region on Sunday and/or Monday. Additionally, with 
precipitable water values progged to approach and even exceed 
2", torrential rainfall will accompany any storms that develop 
and could result in flash flooding wherever storms persist for 
a sufficiently long period of time. With this potential
thunderstorm time window still being 3-4 days out, it remains
practically impossible to pinpoint precisely where and when 
such threats may materialize in the region, and it's entirely 
within the realm of possibility at this point for this
thunderstorm activity to avoid our area altogether (though this
isn't a scenario that we'd bet on based on the look of this 
forthcoming weather pattern). The main message at this point in 
time is that conditions will be favorable for multiple rounds of
severe thunderstorms somewhere in the general region on Sunday 
and on Monday, but specific details regarding this severe 
thunderstorm potential remain highly uncertain at this time.

Forecast confidence from Tuesday onward also remains relatively
low, in part due to the uncertainties with what will happen in 
the preceding days. Ensemble guidance generally favors midweek 
conditions that aren't as hot and humid compared to Sunday and 
Monday, and this outcome would be likely to come to fruition if 
extensive thunderstorm activity materializes on Sunday and/or 
Monday and shunts the muggiest air well to our south and/or 
east.

Ogorek
